title: A community
hookLine: a congregation, sangha, circle or group: the first Christians kept at fellowship and bread daily, and Buddhists take refuge in the sangha
tomorrow: a rabbi prayed his rough neighbors would die. what did his wife say?

cards: A gym membership that hasn't been used since spring. A group chat that went quiet. It's easy to belong to things on paper.
In the book of Acts, the first followers of Jesus had just been through Pentecost, wind and fire and a crowd of new believers. The question was what they'd do on an ordinary Tuesday after that.
Luke answers in one line: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

teach.b: Four things, kept at: the teaching, the fellowship, the bread, the prayers.

And a few verses on, the same people, "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." Daily. In houses.

With gladness. Christians read this as a picture of what a church is: not first a building, but people who keep showing up for each other, around a table, around prayer. A neighbor says something close.
Buddhists take three refuges, and in Pali the third goes: "Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi."

teach.h: I GO TO THE SANGHA FOR REFUGE.
teach.b: I go to the sangha for refuge. The community stands beside the Buddha and his teaching as one of the three jewels. That's what's shared: on both paths, the gathering is something kept at, not joined once.
And one honest difference. The first Christians gathered around Jesus, whom they proclaimed risen, and around the broken bread, as one body.
For Buddhists, the sangha is a refuge beside the Buddha and the Dharma, and the word can mean the order of monks and nuns, or a community of practice.
Different centers, and each named as its own.
On both, belonging grows by returning.

how: Christians gather as churches for teaching, fellowship, the bread and prayer. Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the sangha, and say the three refuges in Pali. People on their own path can find a circle or group to return to.

o: a group you keep returning to on the path
a building where religious services are held
an online audience that follows one teacher

games.q: two kinds of belonging: tap the pairs.
p: I go to the sangha for refuge

s: a community is a nice extra beside the real spiritual path
in Acts the fellowship is one of the four things they kept at; for Buddhists the sangha is one of three refuges.
Acts says the first believers broke bread daily, from house to house
the Christian church and the Buddhist sangha are simply the same thing
the church gathers around the risen Jesus as one body; the sangha is a refuge beside the Buddha and the Dharma.

games.q: your friend went to a meditation group once, felt awkward, and wants to quit. by Acts 2 and the refuge in the sangha, what's the wise next step?
o: go back a few more times: belonging grows by returning.
quit; a real community feels like home on the very first visit.
keep the membership but stop going; belonging on paper is enough.
games.why: They "continued stedfastly" and met daily. On both paths, the community is something you keep returning to.

practice: Choose one gathering you could visit: a congregation, a sangha, a circle, a group that reads or walks. Name the day and the place to yourself, and the one thing most likely to stop you.
Decide what you'll do if it does, then rest in that decision.

wordCard.voice: A community: a congregation, sangha, circle or group you keep returning to, the way the first Christians broke bread daily and Buddhists go to the sangha for refuge.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit, Buddhist: 'assembly', the community, one of the three jewels.

carryVoice: Your line: belong. Not on paper; by returning, from house to house. Day 1658, and the week is nearly whole.
